questions.question: By 322 BCE, who had unified the fragmented territories into the first pan-Indian empire?
questions.explanation: By 322 BCE Chandragupta Maurya had built the first pan-Indian empire.

questions.question: Which roles did the Mauryan state play in trade and commerce? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The four roles were regulator, investor, revenue collector and diplomat.

questions.question: Match each role of the Mauryan state with what it did.
questions.explanation: These are the four roles on the session's slide.
pairs: Set prices, standardized weights and policed hoarding and fraud
Opened and protected markets through treaties and embassies

questions.question: A state that sets prices, standardizes weights and polices hoarding and fraud is acting as a:
questions.explanation: Regulating prices, weights and fraud is the regulator role.

questions.question: The state builds and maintains roads, ports and irrigation that merchants depend on. Which role is this?
questions.explanation: Building roads, ports and irrigation is the investor role.

questions.question: The state taxes agricultural produce and collects tolls to fund administration and the army. Which role is this?
questions.explanation: Taxing production, tolls and trade is the revenue collector role.

questions.question: The state sends an embassy to a foreign king to open and protect markets for its merchants. Which role is this?
questions.explanation: Opening and protecting external markets through treaties and embassies is the diplomat role.

questions.question: The Mauryan state played four roles: regulator, investor, revenue collector and ______.
questions.explanation: Diplomat is the fourth role.

questions.question: The Mauryan state left trade entirely to merchants and guilds, as earlier regional kingdoms had done.
questions.explanation: False. Unlike earlier regional kingdoms, the Mauryan state took a direct, hands-on role in the economy rather than leaving trade to merchants and guilds alone.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the four roles of the Mauryan state in the session?
questions.explanation: The roles are regulator, investor, revenue collector and diplomat.

questions.question: How does the regulator role differ from the investor role?
questions.explanation: Regulation concerns rules and policing; investment concerns building infrastructure.
options: The regulator sets and polices rules on prices, weights and fraud; the investor builds infrastructure like roads and ports
The regulator builds roads and ports; the investor sets prices and polices fraud
Both roles only collect taxes and tolls from traders and farmers
The regulator signs treaties with foreign kings; the investor collects tolls

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The Mauryan state acted as an investor in trade.
Reason (R): It built and maintained the roads, ports and irrigation that trade depended on.
questions.explanation: Both are true and the second explains the first.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.question: Mauryan provinces were run by governors who were often:
questions.explanation: Provinces were run by governors, often princes called kumaras.

questions.question: A kumara in the Mauryan system was a:
questions.explanation: The key terms list defines a kumara as a royal prince appointed as provincial governor.
options: A superintendent who collected tolls at the city gates
A Greek ambassador sent to the court at Pataliputra
Royal prince appointed as a provincial governor
A chief spy who reported on markets and officials

questions.question: The Arthashastra served the Mauryan state as:
questions.explanation: It prescribed rules for revenue, trade and administration.

questions.question: Adhyakshas were ______ who oversaw state departments.
questions.explanation: An adhyaksha is a superintendent or head of a state department.

questions.question: What did the gudhapurushas do?
questions.explanation: Gudhapurushas were spies who reported to the centre.
options: Collected tolls at ferries and river crossings
Led caravans of merchants along the northern road
Minted the coins used in the provincial markets
Reported on prices, markets and the conduct of officials

questions.question: Mauryan adhyakshas answered to an elected legislature.
questions.explanation: False. They answered only to the emperor; modern ministries answer to elected legislatures.

questions.question: A secret agent reports to the capital that grain prices at a border market have suddenly jumped. Which Mauryan institution is at work?
questions.explanation: Spies reported on prices, markets and officials.

questions.question: A prince governing a province makes market decisions without waiting for the capital. Which feature of the Mauryan system does this show?
questions.explanation: Governors pushed decisions closer to markets.
options: Rule by an elected council of merchants in each province
Provincial governors pushing decisions closer to markets
Abolition of provinces so that all decisions are made at Pataliputra
Guild control of the state through the guild councils

questions.question: How do the roles of an adhyaksha and a gudhapurusha differ?
questions.explanation: Adhyakshas oversaw departments; gudhapurushas reported to the centre.
options: An adhyaksha was a spy; a gudhapurusha headed a department of the state
Both were provincial governors, usually chosen from among the princes
Both were foreign envoys sent by the Hellenistic kings
An adhyaksha headed a department; a gudhapurusha was a spy reporting on markets and officials

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a feature of Mauryan centralized administration in the session?
questions.explanation: Adhyakshas answered only to the emperor.
options: Provincial governors, often princes, running the provinces
Adhyakshas overseeing commerce, tolls, mines and ports
A spy network reporting on prices and officials

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Mauryan provinces were run by governors, often princes (kumaras).
Reason (R): Kautilya's Arthashastra functioned as a manual of economic governance.
questions.explanation: Both are true, but the Arthashastra's role as a governance manual does not explain why governors were often princes.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.question: Which features made the Mauryan political economy centralized? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Provinces, the Arthashastra, adhyakshas and spies formed the centralized system.
options: The Arthashastra as a governance manual
Private guild courts that overruled the emperor

questions.question: Match each superintendent with his domain.
questions.explanation: These are the select adhyakshas in the session.

questions.question: The Panyadhyaksha was the Superintendent of:
questions.explanation: Panyadhyaksha was the Superintendent of Commerce.

questions.question: The Sulkadhyaksha oversaw:
questions.explanation: Sulkadhyaksha was the Superintendent of Tolls.

questions.question: The Pautavadhyaksha oversaw:
questions.explanation: Pautavadhyaksha was the Superintendent of Weights and Measures.

questions.question: The Akaradhyaksha oversaw the state monopoly over:
questions.explanation: Akaradhyaksha was the Superintendent of Mines.

questions.question: The Navadhyaksha was the Superintendent of:
questions.explanation: Navadhyaksha was the Superintendent of Ships.

questions.question: Match each Mauryan capital with its position.
questions.explanation: These are the imperial capital and four provincial capitals.

questions.question: Which city was the imperial capital of the Mauryan Empire?
questions.explanation: Pataliputra was the imperial capital.

questions.question: What does the name Suvarnagiri literally mean?
questions.explanation: The session notes that its name literally means mountain of gold.

questions.question: Why was Suvarnagiri economically vital, according to the session?
questions.explanation: Deccan's gold and gems made it vital.
options: The Deccan's mineral wealth, including gold and gems
It held the largest port in the north

questions.question: A merchant needs to know who sets the standard units used in the marketplace. Which official is responsible?
questions.explanation: Pautavadhyaksha oversaw standard units of weights and measures.

questions.question: A boatman runs a ferry at a river crossing and uses a port. Under which superintendent does the session place ports and ferries?
questions.explanation: Navadhyaksha supervised ships, ports, ferries and transport.

questions.question: A trader hauls goods through a city gate and a ford and must pay customs. Which superintendent's office collects this?
questions.explanation: Sulkadhyaksha oversaw tolls and customs duties.

questions.question: Which pairing of superintendent and domain is INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: Akaradhyaksha oversaw mines; ships were under the Navadhyaksha.

questions.question: How does the Panyadhyaksha differ from the Sulkadhyaksha?
questions.explanation: Commerce regulation and toll collection were separate offices.
options: The Panyadhyaksha ran the mines; the Sulkadhyaksha ran the ports and ferries
The Panyadhyaksha regulated trade and merchants; the Sulkadhyaksha collected tolls and customs
Both officials ran the state mines under one shared office
The Panyadhyaksha collected tolls; the Sulkadhyaksha set standard weights

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Suvarnagiri was economically vital to the Mauryan Empire.
Reason (R): Its name literally means 'mountain of silver'.
questions.explanation: A is true. R is false: Suvarnagiri literally means 'mountain of gold'.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.question: A prospector reports a rich gold seam in the Deccan. Under which Mauryan office would the state's monopoly over such minerals fall?
questions.explanation: Mines were under the Akaradhyaksha, with a state monopoly over minerals.
options: The Navadhyaksha, the Superintendent of Ships
The Akaradhyaksha, the Superintendent of Mines
The Panyadhyaksha, the Superintendent of Commerce
The Pautavadhyaksha, the Superintendent of Weights

questions.question: What formed the state's revenue, according to the session?
questions.explanation: Revenue came from a share of land produce and tolls on goods.
options: Tribute paid by Roman merchants and nothing else
Gifts from guild treasurers and nothing else
Fines imposed on priests and nothing else
A share of agricultural produce plus tolls (sulka) on goods

questions.question: Which tools did the Mauryan state use besides revenue collection? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The state paired revenue with price regulation, anti-hoarding and standard weights, measures and currency.

questions.question: Tolls on goods moving through the empire were called ______.
questions.explanation: The session uses the term sulka for tolls on goods moving through the empire, one of the state's main sources of revenue.

questions.question: Common weights, measures and currency reduced transaction costs across a vast territory.
questions.explanation: True. Standardization reduced transaction costs.

questions.question: Merchants withhold stock of an essential good to push up its price. Which Mauryan measure addresses this?
questions.explanation: Rules discouraged merchants from withholding stock to inflate prices.

questions.question: Officials fix the price of an essential commodity to prevent exploitation. Which tool is this?
questions.explanation: Officials monitored and, where needed, fixed prices of essential commodities.

questions.question: How does land revenue differ from tolls in the Mauryan revenue system?
questions.explanation: The two were distinct sources of revenue.
options: Land revenue was charged at ports; tolls were charged on farms
Both were charged only on mines, ships and ferries
Land revenue: a share of produce; tolls: charges on goods moving through the empire
They were the same payment under two different names

questions.question: Which of these is NOT named as a source of Mauryan revenue?
questions.explanation: The session names a share of land produce, tolls and trade.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Standardization reduced transaction costs in the Mauryan Empire.
Reason (R): Common weights, measures and currency made trade across a diverse territory easier.
questions.explanation: Both are true and the second explains the first.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.question: The term sulka refers to:
questions.explanation: Sulka means tolls on goods moving through the empire, one of the state's main sources of revenue.

questions.question: The Uttarapatha in the Mauryan context ran from Pataliputra through Taxila to:
questions.explanation: It ran from Pataliputra through Taxila to the north-west frontier.

questions.question: The Dakshinapatha linked the Gangetic plains to:
questions.explanation: It was the Southern Route to the Deccan plateau.

questions.question: Which goods did the Dakshinapatha carry? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The Dakshinapatha carried gold, gems and spices.

questions.question: The Uttarapatha was the main artery for which trade?
questions.explanation: It carried Central Asian and Hellenistic trade.

questions.question: The Uttarapatha was the route that carried gold, gems and spices.
questions.explanation: False. The Uttarapatha carried Central Asian and Hellenistic trade; the Dakshinapatha carried gold, gems and spices.

questions.question: The Mauryan arterial roads are described as a precursor to today's:
questions.explanation: The session calls the roads a precursor to the Grand Trunk Road.

questions.question: Which supporting infrastructure is named? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: Support included rest houses, wells, garrisoned outposts, river transport, ports and irrigation.

questions.question: State-built roads turned scattered regional markets into one connected ______ network.
questions.explanation: The roads connected scattered regional markets into one trading network.

questions.question: A merchant travels from Pataliputra through Taxila towards the north-west frontier. Which route is he using?
questions.explanation: The Uttarapatha ran from Pataliputra through Taxila to the north-west.

questions.question: Why would a state invest in irrigation along trade roads, not just in the roads themselves?
questions.explanation: Irrigation supports agricultural surplus that is traded along the roads.
options: Irrigation replaces the need for roads, because water carries goods
Roads cannot carry grain, so only river transport matters
Agricultural surplus becomes tradeable goods, so infrastructure investment compounds across sectors
Irrigation was meant only for temples and royal gardens

questions.question: How do the Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha differ in the Mauryan period?
questions.explanation: They served different regions and goods.
options: Uttarapatha: north-west and Hellenistic trade; Dakshinapatha: Deccan gold, gems and spices
The Uttarapatha led to the Deccan; the Dakshinapatha led to Taxila
Both led only to the east coast and to no other region
The Uttarapatha was a sea route; the Dakshinapatha a river route

questions.question: Garrisoned outposts along routes provided security for traders.
questions.explanation: True. They are listed among supporting infrastructure.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT listed as supporting infrastructure for the roads?
questions.explanation: Roman-built harbours are not mentioned.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Mauryan roads left regional markets disconnected from each other.
Reason (R): The state built and maintained arterial roads.
questions.explanation: A is false: the roads converted scattered regional markets into one connected trading network. R is true.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.question: Converting scattered regional markets into one connected network by building roads is an example of the state acting as an:
questions.explanation: Building infrastructure is the investor role.

questions.question: In the treaty with Seleucus I Nicator, Chandragupta secured territory up to the:
questions.explanation: The treaty gave territory up to the Hindu Kush.

questions.question: How many war elephants did Chandragupta give in exchange, according to Session 11?
questions.explanation: The treaty exchanged territory for 500 war elephants.

questions.question: The treaty with Seleucus was sealed with a:
questions.explanation: A marriage alliance sealed the treaty.

questions.question: Megasthenes, who lived at Pataliputra, was the ambassador of:
questions.explanation: Megasthenes was Seleucus's ambassador at Pataliputra.

questions.question: Megasthenes wrote the fragmentary account called the ______.
questions.explanation: His Indica is a key external source on Mauryan administration and trade.

questions.question: Deimachus served as Antiochus I's ambassador at whose court?
questions.explanation: Deimachus continued friendly relations at Bindusara's court.

questions.question: Which five Hellenistic kings did Ashoka's envoys reach, according to Rock Edict XIII? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: The five kings were Antiochus II, Ptolemy II, Antigonus II, Magas and Alexander of Epirus.

questions.question: Ashoka's envoys reached ______ Hellenistic kings, according to Rock Edict XIII.
questions.explanation: Rock Edict XIII names five Hellenistic kings.

questions.question: Session 11 dates the treaty with Seleucus I Nicator to about 303 BCE.
questions.explanation: True. This is the date given in the session.

questions.question: A Greek ambassador resident at Pataliputra writes an account of Mauryan administration. Who is he, and why is his work valuable?
questions.explanation: Megasthenes's fragmentary Indica remains a key external source.
options: Megasthenes; his Indica is a key external source
Deimachus; his edicts founded the empire
Seleucus; his treaty ended the empire
Antiochus II; his coins fixed prices

questions.question: How do Megasthenes and Deimachus differ?
questions.explanation: They represented different Seleucid kings at different Mauryan courts.
options: Megasthenes served at Bindusara's court; Deimachus served at Chandragupta's
Both men served at the court of Ashoka after the Kalinga War
Both men were Mauryan governors of provinces in the north-west
Megasthenes was Seleucus's ambassador at Pataliputra; Deimachus was Antiochus I's ambassador at Bindusara's court

questions.question: Which of these is NOT among the five Hellenistic kings of Rock Edict XIII?
questions.explanation: Seleucus I was the treaty partner of Chandragupta, not one of the five kings.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Embassies routinely doubled as commercial and intelligence channels.
Reason (R): Ashoka's envoys reached five Hellenistic kings, according to Rock Edict XIII.
questions.explanation: Both are true, but the number of kings reached does not explain why embassies doubled as commercial and intelligence channels.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.question: Which Mauryan ruler made the treaty with Seleucus I Nicator?
questions.explanation: Chandragupta made the treaty.

questions.question: Match each person with their role or period in the session.
questions.explanation: These come from the people-behind-the-Mauryan-economy slide.
pairs: Founded the empire, r. c. 322-297 BCE
Maintained Hellenistic ties, r. c. 297-268 BCE

questions.question: Who founded the Mauryan Empire with Kautilya as chief advisor?
questions.explanation: Chandragupta founded the empire.

questions.question: Kautilya is described as the:
questions.explanation: Kautilya wrote the Arthashastra, which shaped Mauryan economic policy.

questions.question: Bindusara is described as the ruler who:
questions.explanation: Bindusara maintained Hellenistic ties.
options: Fought the Kalinga War and then turned to a policy of welfare
Founded the empire and unified the fragmented kingdoms
Maintained Hellenistic diplomatic ties and hosted Deimachus
Wrote the Arthashastra as a manual of economic governance

questions.question: Ashoka pivoted to a welfare policy after which event?
questions.explanation: The Kalinga War was the catalyst for Ashoka's welfare policy shift.

questions.question: The Kalinga War of about 261 BCE was a turning point towards ______ policy.
questions.explanation: The Kalinga War was a turning point toward Dhamma and welfare policy.

questions.question: Which came first?
questions.explanation: The treaty comes first in the timeline.
options: The fall of the Mauryas (c. 185 BCE)

questions.question: Which sequence is in correct order?
questions.explanation: The dates are c. 268, c. 261, c. 250 and c. 232 BCE.
options: Kalinga War, Ashoka ascends, death of Ashoka, embassies
Death of Ashoka, Kalinga War, Ashoka ascends, embassies
Embassies, Ashoka ascends, death of Ashoka, Kalinga War
Ashoka ascends, Kalinga War, embassies to Hellenistic kings, death of Ashoka

questions.question: The Mauryan Empire fell about:
questions.explanation: The fall of the Mauryas is dated about 185 BCE.

questions.question: Ashoka died around 268 BCE.
questions.explanation: False. About 268 BCE is when Ashoka ascended the throne; he died around 232 BCE.

questions.question: A historian describes a ruler who expanded connectivity through infrastructure and embassies and then pivoted to welfare policy. Who is described?
questions.explanation: This describes Ashoka, who expanded connectivity through infrastructure and embassies and pivoted to welfare policy after the Kalinga War.

questions.question: A source says: 'Founded the empire, unified fragmented kingdoms with Kautilya as chief advisor, and made a treaty with Seleucus.' Which ruler is described?
questions.explanation: These are the details given for Chandragupta.

questions.question: Which pairing of person and role is INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: Chandragupta founded the empire; Bindusara succeeded him.
options: Ashoka: pivoted to welfare after Kalinga

questions.question: How do Chandragupta's and Ashoka's contributions differ?
questions.explanation: The session assigns them different roles.
options: Chandragupta fought the Kalinga War; Ashoka founded the empire
Both founded the empire and both made the Seleucus treaty
Chandragupta founded the empire; Ashoka expanded connectivity and turned to welfare
Ashoka made the Seleucus treaty; Chandragupta shifted to welfare

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Ashoka's policy shifted towards welfare after the Kalinga War.
Reason (R): The Kalinga War took place after Ashoka's death.
questions.explanation: A is true. R is false: the Kalinga War (about 261 BCE) came during his reign and was the catalyst for the shift.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.question: The Mauryan Empire fell around 185 ______.
questions.explanation: The fall of the Mauryas is dated about 185 BCE, roughly half a century after the death of Ashoka about 232 BCE.

questions.question: Who succeeded Chandragupta around 297 BCE?
questions.explanation: Chandragupta was succeeded by Bindusara.

questions.question: Which event is dated about 250 BCE?
questions.explanation: Embassies reached Hellenistic kings and Sri Lanka about 250 BCE.
options: Embassies reach Hellenistic kings and Sri Lanka
The Kalinga War, a turning point towards welfare policy
The fall of the Mauryas, the end of the empire
The founding of the empire by Chandragupta Maurya

questions.question: Match each Mauryan feature with its modern equivalent.
questions.explanation: The session frames the Mauryan state as having the same functions with different tools.
pairs: Bilateral trade agreements and foreign missions

questions.question: Where does the Mauryan-modern analogy break, according to the session?
questions.explanation: Adhyakshas answered only to the emperor, while modern ministries answer to elected legislatures, so accountability is where the analogy breaks.
options: Modern states have no roads, while Mauryan states had many
Mauryan states had no diplomacy, while modern states have it
Adhyakshas were elected by the people, like modern ministers
Adhyakshas answered only to the emperor, while modern ministries answer to elected legislatures

questions.question: Modern ministries answer to elected legislatures.
questions.explanation: True. This is where the analogy with the Mauryan system breaks.

questions.question: Mauryan centralized administration corresponds to:
questions.explanation: Centralized administration corresponds to national ministries and regulators.
options: Bilateral trade agreements with foreign states
Tolls collected at modern ports and airports

questions.question: Mauryan roads correspond to modern national ______ and logistics infrastructure.
questions.explanation: Roads correspond to national highways and logistics infrastructure in the session's Mauryan-versus-modern comparison.

questions.question: A government signs a bilateral trade agreement and opens a foreign mission to help its exporters. Which Mauryan function does this parallel?
questions.explanation: Diplomatic relations correspond to bilateral trade agreements and foreign missions.

questions.question: A minister today must explain a market policy to Parliament, while a Mauryan superintendent explained his to the emperor. Which point does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Accountability is the difference.
options: The two systems are identical in every feature of accountability
Both had elected legislatures holding officials to account
Neither system had officials responsible for the economy
Where the analogy breaks: to whom officials are accountable

questions.question: How do Mauryan adhyakshas differ from modern ministries in accountability?
questions.explanation: This is the break in the analogy.
options: Adhyakshas answered only to the emperor; ministries answer to elected legislatures
Adhyakshas answered to legislatures; ministries answer to emperors
Both answered to the guilds that regulated the markets
Both answered to Rome, which set the rules for trade

questions.question: Which pairing of Mauryan feature and modern equivalent is INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: Diplomacy corresponds to bilateral agreements and foreign missions.
options: Centralized administration: national ministries and regulators

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Session 11 says Mauryan adhyakshas answered to elected legislatures.
Reason (R): Modern ministries answer to elected legislatures.
questions.explanation: A is false: adhyakshas answered only to the emperor. R is true.
options: Both A and R are true, and R explains A
Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.question: Which pairings are made in the session? (Select all that apply)
questions.explanation: These are the three pairings.
options: Diplomatic relations with bilateral trade agreements

questions.question: What question does the session pose at the start, which students should be able to answer by the end?
questions.explanation: The framing answer is centralized political economy, road networks and diplomatic relations.
options: Why did the Kushanas rise to control the Silk Route?
How did guild banks lend money to merchants?
What factors made the Mauryan Empire an economic powerhouse?
Why did Rome import pepper from the Malabar Coast?

cards.front: Four roles of the Mauryan state
cards.back: Regulator (prices, weights, hoarding, fraud); Investor (roads, ports, irrigation); Revenue collector (production, tolls, trade); Diplomat (treaties and embassies).
Panyadhyaksha: commerce. Sulkadhyaksha: tolls. Pautavadhyaksha: weights and measures. Akaradhyaksha: mines. Navadhyaksha: ships, ports, ferries.
Pataliputra (imperial centre), Taxila (north-west), Ujjain (west, Malwa), Tosali (east, Kalinga), Suvarnagiri (south, Deccan).
Seleucus I treaty c. 303 BCE: territory up to the Hindu Kush for 500 war elephants plus a marriage alliance. Megasthenes (Indica). Deimachus. Five kings in Rock Edict XIII.
c. 322 founding; c. 303 Seleucus treaty; c. 297 Bindusara; c. 268 Ashoka; c. 261 Kalinga War; c. 250 embassies; c. 232 Ashoka dies; c. 185 BCE fall.
